The Biggest Takeaway From Palantir Technologies’ Latest Quarterly Report Is a Potential Warning Sign Investors Shouldn’t Miss
Harsh Chauhan, The Motley Fool

PLTR

Trading disclosure

Palantir Technologies (NASDAQ:PLTR) has been at the forefront of the artificial intelligence (AI) software revolution over the past three years, with the company's AI platform in solid demand from both commercial and government customers.

So, when Palantir released its third-quarter results on Nov. 2, it was easy to see why the company's revenue and earnings grew at an incredible pace. What's more, Palantir raised its full-year guidance once again, driven by the exceptional growth in the company's U.S. commercial business.

Missed Nvidia in 2009? This Rare Signal Is Flashing Again. In 2009, a "Double Down" signal flashed for a little-known chipmaker called Nvidia. For the first time in years, that same "Total Conviction" signal is flashing for a company 1/100th the size of Nvidia. Continue »

However, Palantir stock slid following its earnings report. Let's see why that was the case and examine a potential red flag that could derail the company's impressive growth trajectory.

Image source: The Motley Fool.

Palantir's quarterly performance was solid, but there is a problem

Palantir's Q3 revenue increased by 96% year over year to $2.3 billion. This was the first time its quarterly revenue crossed the $2 billion milestone. Even better, the company's adjusted earnings per share (EPS) increased by 109% year over year to $0.44. Palantir's revenue and earnings exceeded Wall Street's expectations.

Palantir benefited from the persistently strong demand for its Artificial Intelligence Platform (AIP), which is helping it win more business from existing customers. Management pointed out several instances during the company's latest earnings call in which customers have awarded Palantir larger contracts following the initial deployment of its AI solutions.

For instance, Palantir noted that a "global athletic company converted a $1.6 million pilot that began in Q1 2026 into an approximately $21 million ACV deal last quarter," where ACV refers to the annual contract value. Management outlined several other examples, indicating that the benefits delivered by Palantir's AI software platform are boosting demand.

This also explains why Palantir increased its annual revenue guidance once again. It now expects $8.53 billion in revenue for 2026, driven by a 143% increase in U.S. commercial revenue to $3.56 billion. The updated guidance implies a 91% increase in Palantir's top line, which would be an improvement over its 2025 growth of 56%.

Meanwhile, the company anticipates adjusted free cash flow of $4.8-$5 billion this year, significantly higher than last year's $2.27 billion. So, there are a lot of positive takeaways from Palantir's latest quarterly report. However, a sharp slowdown in new contracts marred the company's impressive performance and strong guidance.

title: Prediction: $5,000 Invested in Palantir Will Be Worth This Much by 2031
detail:
Prediction: $5,000 Invested in Palantir Will Be Worth This Much by 2031
Will Healy, The Motley Fool
Fri, November 6, 2026 at 5:53 AM MST 6 min read
PLTR
Trade PLTR on Coinbase
Trading disclosure

Palantir (NASDAQ: PLTR) has become a phenomenally successful investment for longer-term shareholders, but also one that is difficult for new buyers to jump into. The stock is up about 25-fold from its December 2022 low. However, its elevated valuation also makes it risky to buy at current levels.

Long-term investors often buy stocks planning to hold them for a minimum of five years. Given that, it may be useful to speculate about where this stock could trade in 2031 and where that outcome would leave the value of a $5,000 investment made in it today. Although a lot could happen during that time that would dramatically alter any forecast we make this month, I think investors should prepare for significant struggles alongside the company's growth. Here's why.

Missed AI's "Act 1"? Act 2 Could Be 16x Bigger. Most investors think they missed the AI boat because they didn't buy Nvidia in 2005. But according to our analysts, we're only at the end of "Act 1"—the R&D phase. "Act 2" is the global rollout. Continue »

Image source: The Motley Fool.
The state of Palantir

Trying to figure out what history says about Palantir can be challenging, though. From a certain perspective, the business can justify the stock's premium. The stock has been a tremendously successful investment because the company has delivered real productivity gains to its clients, particularly on the commercial side of its business.

One example is Citibank's CitiWealth, which used Palantir's software to streamline the onboarding process for new customers. This reduced the onboarding time for the most complex accounts from nine days to seconds. Now, a single employee can handle everything related to opening an account. Previously, 50 were involved in the process.

Also, the U.K.'s National Health Service is using Palantir's software to plan staffing, monitor patient demand, and track where hospital beds are available. This allows for more efficient resource allocation, reducing bottlenecks and shortening wait times.

Such productivity gains helped Palantir increase its revenue by 92% year over year in the first nine months of 2026. Due to a more modest rise in its costs and expenses, its profits during that time surged by 201% to almost $3.1 billion.

Projecting Palantir in 2031

Though the AI data analytics company has been growing impressively, any forecast about what its growth might look like over the next five years will require a large dose of guesswork. The average forecast among analysts today is for an 84% revenue increase this year, then a deceleration to 51% growth in 2027. Grand View Research forecasts a 31% compound annual growth rate for the overall artificial intelligence industry through 2033. Since we do not have company-specific revenue forecasts for Palantir beyond 2027, that might be an appropriate estimate for its growth in the period ahead.

Snowflake (SNOW) stock fell 7.2% on Thursday, November 5, 2026, while the S&P 500 lost 4.4%. The company released no earnings reports or filings around the drop, which occurred in a session when the Nasdaq Composite fell 5.5%. What does Snowflake do, and did the stock fall on its own or with its group?

Management Credits AI For Faster Snowflake Growth

Snowflake is a technology company that operates the AI Data Cloud, a data platform for businesses. Management has tied the company's recent pickup in growth to AI. Product revenue grew 37% from a year earlier in fiscal Q2 2027, marking the third straight quarter in which growth sped up, management said on the September 2, 2026 call.

Newer products, such as AI functions and the AI gateway, contributed approximately half of that speed-up, management said on the same call. Citing strength in both its core data platform and its AI business, management also raised its product revenue forecast for fiscal 2027 to $6.07 billion. For a holder, the AI tie makes Snowflake partly a bet on businesses using AI on its platform.

Snowflake Fell Along With Technology Stocks

While Snowflake fell more than the S&P 500, its drop was smaller than the 8.0% fall in the SPDR technology sector fund (XLK) that session. Among the peers Trefis tracks for Snowflake, Palantir Technologies fell 9.7%, while Oracle, Microsoft, Amazon.com and Alphabet all fell less than Snowflake. The stock moved with technology stocks as a group, not on its own.

For the market, days like this are rare. After the 21 before November 5, the week ahead was a coin flip.

Where Snowflake Stock Stands Now

Big drops are not rare for Snowflake. Over the past year, the stock had 10 sessions with a fall at least this large. The latest came on October 30, 2026, when it lost 7.3%.

Over the past 12 months, Snowflake stock returned 1.6%, against 9.9% for the S&P 500. The stock swung widely over that year, posting its lowest close of $121.11 on April 10, 2026, and its highest of $368.89 on October 9, 2026. It closed at $269.54 on November 5. Over the past month, the stock lost 19.0%, against a 5.7% fall for the S&P 500.

At its November 5 close, Snowflake was valued at 17.3 times its sales over the past twelve months, against 3.2 times for the S&P 500.

Snowflake is expected to report its fiscal third-quarter 2027 results in December 2026. Product revenue growth, which management guided to 37% to 38% for that quarter, is the measure to watch.

Palantir (NASDAQ:PLTR) trades at $154.45, and Wall Street's average price target is $217.97. That implies 41.1% upside to where analysts think it should be.

gorodenkoff / Getty Images

Palantir sells data-integration and AI software (Foundry, Ontology and AIP) to governments and, more and more, to corporations. Wall Street keeps watching because of the pace of its growth. Revenue rose 95.9% year over year last quarter to $2.31 billion.

Some desks see much more upside. Barclays raised its target from $265 to $273 and kept its Overweight rating. That target implies 76.8% upside. A consensus gap above 40% shows a wide split between the market price and analyst models.

A Blowout Quarter Ran Into a 21% One-Week Slide

Valuation fatigue is the main reason the stock fell. It met a risk-off market right after a record earnings report. Shares fell 10.05% on the day and 21.37% over the past week. Yet the results beat estimates. Adjusted EPS of $0.44 exceeded the $0.41 consensus, and management raised full-year revenue guidance to $8.530 billion to $8.534 billion. Axios summed up the mood with the headline "Palantir loses its wow factor".

Bears zeroed in on a few weak spots. Total contract value grew only 6% year over year. Stock-based compensation rose to $318.9 million from $172.3 million. Accounts receivable jumped to $1.883 billion from $1.042 billion at the end of 2025. At roughly 82x forward earnings, even small defects get hurt.

The broader market fell too. The S&P 500 dropped 4.22% in the session and 4.53% over the week. Palantir fell much further.
